title: Hook: The Mystery of the Missing Clocks
text: Imagine waking up in a world where every single clock, watch, and smartphone has suddenly vanished. There are no alarms to wake you up, no bells to signal the end of a school period, and no timers for cooking. How would you know when to eat, sleep, or meet your friends?

title: Socratic Thinking: What would happen?
text: Before you scroll down, take a moment to think. If you were completely lost in a forest with no watch, how would you figure out what time of day it is? What clues does nature provide?

content.title: Discovery: Nature's Timekeeper
content.description: Watch how the length and direction of a shadow change as the sun moves across the sky.

title: Reveal: Sundials, The First Clocks
text: Thousands of years ago, people noticed that the sun's position creates shadows that move in a predictable pattern. They invented the Sundial, a device that tells time based on the position of the sun. The shadow of a pointer (called a gnomon) falls on a marked surface to indicate the hour.

content.question: At what time of day will a sundial's shadow be the shortest?

title: Reflection: Limitations of Sun-Time
text: Think about it: why doesn't a sundial work at night? Or on a very cloudy day? If you were living in ancient times, how would you measure time when the sun isn't shining?

title: Connection: The Moon and Stars
text: The sun helps us track hours in a day, but what about tracking months and years? Just as the sun's daily path creates a day, the changing phases of the moon help us track months, and the changing positions of star constellations help us track the seasons and years. This connects directly to our earlier studies on the Solar System and planetary motions.

content.title: Mastery: Build Your Own Sundial
content.description: Take a paper plate, a pencil, and some clay. Stick the pencil in the center of the plate using the clay. Place it outside in a sunny spot on a weekend. Every hour, mark where the pencil's shadow falls. You've just built your very own timekeeping device! Track it for a whole day to see time in action.

content.title: Historical Context
content.text: Remind students that different ancient civilizations, like the Egyptians and the Indians at Jantar Mantar, built massive sundials and observatories that were incredibly accurate, long before modern mechanical clocks existed.

content.title: Confusing Seasons with Daily Time
content.text: Remember, the Earth's rotation on its axis causes day and night (daily time), while the Earth's revolution around the Sun causes a year and seasons. The moon's revolution around the Earth gives us a month.
